cues.text: A Sick Child's Vow
Adalbert was born Vojtech around 956 in Libice, Bohemia, into the powerful Slavnik family, rivals to the ruling Premyslid dynasty for influence in the region.
According to tradition, his parents feared a childhood illness seemed likely to kill him and vowed to raise him for the Church if he recovered.
They kept the vow, sending him to study at Magdeburg under Archbishop Adalbert.
The young Vojtech took his name as his own upon being confirmed.
He returned to Bohemia, was ordained a priest around the age of twenty-five, and in 983, remarkably young for the office, was named bishop of Prague.
A Reformer Twice Driven Out
Adalbert's episcopate collided almost immediately with clergy and nobility unwilling to accept the discipline he tried to impose.
Resistance to his campaigns against polygamy, the slave trade, and clerical laxity grew serious enough that he fled Prague for Rome within a few years of his consecration.
He entered the monastery of Sts.
Boniface and Alexius on the Aventine and, for a time, lived in the humblest tasks of the house rather than as a bishop.
Released by Pope John XV from his episcopal obligations, he might have remained a monk indefinitely.
But his own people, missing him, pressed for his return—only to drive him out a second time when the same underlying resistance to reform resurfaced.
Missionary to Hungary and Poland
Rather than force a third return to a diocese that plainly did not want him, Adalbert turned outward, becoming a missionary to peoples just beginning to enter the Christian fold.
He preached in Hungary during the reign of the pagan chieftain Geza, and tradition holds that Adalbert baptized both Geza and his young son.
Though its precise details are disputed by later historians, tradition identifies that son as the future St.
Stephen of Hungary , who would complete the Christianization of the Magyar people.
Adalbert's own brief mission had helped set that process in motion.
He then moved on to Poland, where he became close to Duke Boleslaw the Brave and was welcomed by Duke Boleslaw the Brave and continued his missionary work in Poland.
Martyrdom on the Baltic Coast
In 997, with Boleslaw's support and a small armed escort, Adalbert set out to evangelize the still-pagan Baltic Prussians, a people who had resisted every previous Christian mission.
His approach involved preaching directly and, by some accounts, relying more on books and formal instruction.
This differed from the persuasive oratory that had served him better in Hungary.
His approach met hostility almost from the start, and local communities repeatedly ordered him to leave their territory.
On 23 April 997, resting after Mass near the coast, Adalbert and his companions were set upon by a group led by a pagan priest named Sicco.
He was speared and beheaded, his head displayed on a pole as a warning against further missionary intrusion.
Legacy
Duke Boleslaw ransomed Adalbert's body from the Prussians for its weight in gold and enshrined it at Gniezno.
There, the cathedral's famous bronze doors still depict eighteen scenes from his life and martyrdom.
Pope Sylvester II canonized him within two years of his death, in 999.

He is honored today as patron of Poland, Bohemia, and Hungary alike — a rare distinction for a saint claimed with equal devotion by three nations he moved among restlessly, welcomed nowhere for long, and served anyway.
We recognize in Adalbert a witness that a reformer's failures do not settle the final verdict on a life given without reservation to the truth it served.
Those failures were two expulsions from his own see and a mission to the Prussians that lasted only weeks.
